content.title: About
content.content: Black beans, also known as black soybeans, are a legume widely used in Mexican, Caribbean, and American cuisines. They have a dense, slightly sweet flesh, a deep black color, and a distinctive earthy aroma. Commonly served as a side dish, in salads, soups, and fast‑food items.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Black beans are rich in anthocyanins, pigments that give them their dark color and act as antioxidants.
In traditional Mexican cooking they are called “frijol” and are a key ingredient in dishes like “frijoles con arroz”.
In Asian restaurants they often appear in “black bean sauce”, a savory alternative to soy sauce.
They provide a substantial amount of plant‑based protein, making them popular in vegetarian and vegan diets.
In the United States black beans are frequently used in fast‑food items such as burritos, tacos, and bean chips.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: One cup of cooked black beans delivers about 15 g of protein, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion, satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains iron and folate
items.content: These nutrients are essential for blood formation and preventing anemia, especially in women of childbearing age.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Anthocyanins and polyphenols protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Black beans raise blood glucose slowly, which is beneficial for people with pre‑diabetes.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Present in beans and can reduce mineral absorption; soaking and cooking lessen its effect.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Legumes may cause gastrointestinal discomfort in sensitive individuals; gradual introduction helps.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: A small percentage of people may experience allergic reactions to beans.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Excessive intake can increase uric acid levels, which may be problematic for gout sufferers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Black beans can be eaten boiled, mashed into spreads, added to salads, soups, chili, burritos, and tacos. They are also enjoyed as a snack when roasted with spices. Before cooking, soak the dry beans for at least 8 hours, then boil until tender.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry beans in an airtight container in a cool, dry place for up to 1 year. Cooked beans keep in the refrigerator for 3–4 days or can be frozen for up to 3 months.
